title: Redwood POC weekly sync - benchmark review vs baseline provider
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark numbers (latency and throughput) comparing Redwood against customer baseline provider. Discussed 95p and 99p latencies, throughput (tokens/sec and concurrent requests), batching effects, KV/prefix cache impact, quantization profiles, and next steps for final run and security handoff.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-27
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Rao, Kaitlyn Wu, Miguel Torres (Redwood); Tom Briggs, Lina Morales, Ethan Park, Priya Desai (Astra Health)

[00:00] Samir: Okay everyone, thanks for joining — this is our weekly POC sync, we'll focus on the benchmark numbers vs your baseline provider and surface tuning options. Tom, you on?
[00:08] Tom: Yep, here. Thanks, Samir. We got the sheet from last week, ran some more tests overnight. Quick heads up, some of our tests had noise from CI jobs, so we filtered a few out.
[00:20] Kaitlyn: Cool, thanks for flagging. We looked at the same runs and also added a couple of dedicated-capacity runs on our side to get stable tail latency. We'll start with the 95p numbers, then 99p and throughput.
[00:35] Lina: Quick question before you start — our primary workload is short responses (avg 48 tokens) but we also have a long form summarization path (avg 320 tokens). We care about both tail latency and tokens/sec for throughput.
[00:48] Miguel: Got it — we tried to mirror that with 64-token and 256-token synthetic sequences. The sheet (link) shows the split.
[01:00] Kaitlyn: Alright, 64-token seqs: Redwood hosted (curated model v1.3, int8 quantized) 95th = 180ms, 99th = 260ms. Baseline provider (their standard endpoint) 95th = 330ms, 99th = 470ms. Throughput at 50 concurrent RPS: Redwood tokens/sec ~12k, baseline ~7.5k. These are median of 3 runs.
[01:28] Ethan: Wait, those 99th numbers are from the same sequence distribution? Baseline seemed to spike with cold-starts earlier.
[01:35] Samir: Good call — we forced warm state across runs by pre-warming KV cache. For the baseline numbers they left cold starts in by default; we re-ran and the gap tightened but Redwood still showed ~150ms 95p improvement and ~120–180ms on 99p.
[01:56] Tom: That's promising. For long sequences (256 tokens), what did you see?
[02:02] Kaitlyn: For 256-token seqs: Redwood 95p = 420ms, 99p = 610ms. Baseline provider 95p = 580ms, 99p = 940ms. Throughput wise at batch size 8, tokens/sec Redwood ~9.2k vs baseline ~6.1k.
[02:24] Lina: Are those with KV cache enabled? Last time the cache made a huge difference for our workload because we have repeated prefixes on prompts.
[02:30] Miguel: Yes, the long-seq runs had prefix/KV cache on. We also toggled cache-off runs — with cache off, Redwood 99p jumped to ~820ms for 256 tokens. So cache is critical for your repeated-context traffic.
[02:47] Priya: From security side, are any logs containing raw prompts in the exported traces? We need to ensure PHI is redacted before sharing with wider team.
[02:55] Samir: The spreadsheet has hashed prompts; raw logs contain prompts but we can provide a redacted set. I'll attach a redacted trace and a sanitized version of the raw.
[03:06] Tom: Nice. Also curious about autoscale behavior — we simulate burst from 50 to 200 concurrent requests. How did Redwood behave?
[03:13] Kaitlyn: Under burst to 200 concurrent, Redwood Dedicated config (simulated on our side) sustained 95p degradation to ~230ms for 64-token seqs and throughput held at ~10k tokens/sec. Baseline provider had more pronounced tail at burst: 95p ~420ms, throughput dropped to ~5k tokens/sec.
[03:32] Ethan: Did you use batching/sharded GPUs for the Dedicated tests?
[03:36] Miguel: We used g4-like instance equivalent with continuous batching and dynamic kernel selection. We also tested a lower-precision fp16 path which reduced average latency ~8% but slightly increased variance on the 99p.
[03:49] Tom: What's the tradeoff there — do we risk quality by going fp16 or int8?
[03:54] Kaitlyn: For your model (we used open model X-2.1 variant), fp16 had negligible quality delta on our eval prompts. int8 quant gave better perf but requires a small eval run for regen and may introduce mild tokenization artifacts in edge cases — we flagged a couple in the sheet. For production we usually recommend fp16 for critical tail stability, int8 where cost matters and you can tolerate rare regressions; we also have rollback policies.
[04:21] Lina: Any numbers for cost delta vs baseline? Rough estimate per 1M tokens?
[04:25] Samir: We put a conservative unit cost in the sheet; Redwood hosted cost per million tokens on that config showed ~18% lower unit cost than baseline for the tested throughput thanks to batching and caching. For Dedicated, unit cost drops further but requires commit.
[04:40] Priya: On Private deployment — what about KMS and audit logs? We need to ensure the logs are forward-compatible with our SIEM.
[04:48] Miguel: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we export audit logs in JSONC that you can ship to Splunk/Datadog. We'll share the integration doc.
[04:56] Priya: Ok please send the doc. Also need an answer on data residency — can you ensure EU region only?
[05:02] Samir: Yes, we can pin region for hosted and Dedicated; Private obviously stays in-cust infra. We'll include a note in the handoff.
[05:10] Tom: Back to perf, what about p99 spikes during re-rollouts or model swaps? Our baseline had periodic degradations when variants rotated.
[05:18] Kaitlyn: We tested model rollouts with canary traffic — Redwood's routing has weighted rollout with automatic fallback to a stable model variant. In our test a bad canary yielded instantaneous fallback; 99p spikes were suppressed because of local early-failover. We can replicate that in your environment.
[05:35] Ethan: One more question on the tokenization differences — the baseline uses their custom tokenizer; we saw minor length diffs. Did you normalize token counts?
[05:42] Miguel: We normalized by giving both systems the same canonical prompt encoding and measuring returned tokens; differences are <3% on average, not material for throughput.
[05:50] Tom: Good. Any surprises in the logs?
[05:53] Kaitlyn: A couple of outliers where latency hit >1.2s during background maintenance windows on baseline. Redwood didn't show that on the same schedule. One caveat: when caching is not helpful (unique, one-off prompts) Redwood's advantage shrinks but still overall better p95/p99 in our runs.
[06:12] Lina: Could you re-run a heavy unique-prompt test for 1 hour? That's closer to our exploratory user traffic.
[06:16] Kaitlyn: Yes — added to next steps, we'll run a 1-hour unique-prompt endurance test and share histograms.
[06:23] Samir: For the numbers we shared, I want to call out environment parity: we matched CPU/Network config as closely as possible but host-level differences exist. The important point is the delta and trend — Redwood reduced tail latency materially in both short and long sequences.
[06:40] Tom: For decision criteria, we need: 1) SLA tail latency numbers (95/99), 2) cost per million tokens, 3) security compliance answers, 4) migration/runbook. We'll use that to sign off for Dedicated pilot.
[06:54] Samir: Noted. We'll provide a one-pager that maps those criteria to the runs.
[07:00] Priya: On the security doc — additionally we need info on data deletion and retention windows.
[07:06] Miguel: Redwood supports configurable retention; we can set zero retention for raw prompts on request and enable meta-metrics only. We'll detail that.
[07:14] Ethan: Would be great to get a microbenchmark for 95p under burst synthetic traffic that more closely simulates our peak — 350 concurrent short requests.
[07:23] Kaitlyn: We'll do a 350-concurrent short-request test using sustained ramp and report both avg and tail. Expectation from current sims: 95p ~260–320ms with Dedicated autoscale; baseline ~450–550ms.
[07:36] Tom: Ok. On pricing, if we move to Dedicated, can we get a short-term commit to match our Q4 forecast? We don't want to overcommit.
[07:45] Samir: We have monthly reserved tiers; we can propose a 3-month pilot commit that gives discounted unit costs without long lock-in. I'll include numbers in the sheet.
[07:57] Lina: One last tech Q — how deterministic is the model-runtime for reproducing odd outputs? We want repeatable inference for debugging.
[08:04] Miguel: We offer deterministic seed options and request-level tracing; however quantized int8 runs may have some non-determinism due to kernel reductions. fp16 is more deterministic. We'll note reproducibility tradeoffs.
[08:20] Tom: Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[08:23] Samir: We'll share the updated spreadsheet and redacted traces by Friday. We'll run the extra endurance and burst tests and post by Saturday. Also we'll schedule the final perf review with your infra folks for Nov 3rd.
[08:35] Priya: We'll verify SOC2 and KMS contacts internally and send them over.
[08:40] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[08:45] — End of recorded transcript —

Notes and known transcription artifacts: occasional speaker overlap, product names sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Dedicated" vs "red wood dedicated", "KV cache" sometimes appears as "K V cache". Numbers are approximate and reflect median of runs; raw logs in drive link contain per-request traces.
